ctw.texte: Many universities are trying to reduce their [[energy]] use. Some have installed solar [[panels]] on the roofs of their buildings, while others have [[changed]] the lights in classrooms to save [[electricity]]. Students are also [[encouraged]] to bring their own water [[bottles]] instead of buying plastic ones. These small [[actions]] can make a big [[difference]] over time, and they help young people [[understand]] how to protect the [[environment]].

Online courses have become very [[popular]] in recent years. Students can watch lectures at any [[moment]], which is useful for people who [[work]] during the day. However, learning alone can be [[difficult]] because there is no teacher in the [[room]] to answer questions. Many courses now offer discussion [[groups]], so that students can share their [[ideas]] and help each [[other]] when a topic is hard to [[follow]].

ap.texte: Bees are among the most important insects for human food production. When a bee visits a flower to collect nectar, grains of pollen stick to its body and are carried to the next flower. This process, called pollination, allows many plants to produce fruit and seeds. Scientists estimate that about one third of the food people eat depends on insect pollination. In recent decades, however, the number of bees has fallen in several countries. Researchers point to the use of certain chemicals on farms, the loss of wild flowers, and diseases that spread among bee colonies. Some farmers have responded by planting strips of wild flowers along their fields, which gives bees food and shelter. Early results suggest that these strips can help bee populations recover, although experts agree that more research is needed.

q.p: What does the passage say pollination allows plants to do?
According to the passage, what share of human food depends on insect pollination?
Which is mentioned as a cause of falling bee numbers?
What do experts say about planting wild flower strips?
o: They may help, but more research is needed

ap.texte: Before the fifteenth century, books in Europe were copied by hand, usually by monks. A single book could take months to produce, so books were rare and expensive. Around 1450, Johannes Gutenberg developed a printing press that used movable metal letters. These letters could be arranged to form a page, inked, and pressed onto paper, and then rearranged to print a different page. The new method made it possible to produce hundreds of copies in a short time. As a result, the price of books fell, and more people learned to read. Historians argue that printing helped ideas spread faster than ever before, contributing to major changes in science, religion and politics. Not everyone welcomed the change: some scribes feared that they would lose their work.

q.p: How were books produced before the fifteenth century?
What was new about Gutenberg's press?
What was one result of printing?
Why did some scribes dislike the new method?

talk.t: Today I want to talk about coral reefs. Many people think corals are plants, but they are actually animals. Each coral is made of tiny creatures called polyps, which live together in large colonies. Corals get most of their energy from algae that live inside their tissue. In return, the corals give the algae a safe place to live. This partnership works well only when the water temperature stays within a narrow range. When the ocean becomes too warm, the corals push out the algae, and they turn white. We call this bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, but it is weak, and if the warm water lasts too long, the coral will die. That is why scientists are worried about rising ocean temperatures.

q.p: What is the main topic of the talk?
o: Coral reefs and what threatens them

q.p: What does the speaker say about corals?
What happens when the water becomes too warm?
Why are scientists worried?

talk.titre: Le marché du travail et les compétences
talk.t: In this lecture I want to look at how technology is changing the skills that employers want. A few decades ago, many jobs required people to repeat the same task all day, for example on a factory line. Today machines do much of that work. As a result, employers are looking for skills that machines do not have: solving unusual problems, working well in a team, and explaining ideas clearly. Some economists call these soft skills. Interestingly, studies show that workers with strong soft skills are more likely to keep their jobs when companies introduce new technology. For students, the lesson is that learning how to learn may be more valuable than memorizing one particular method.

q.p: What is the lecture mainly about?
o: Skills employers want in a changing job market

q.p: What do machines now do?
Which is mentioned as a soft skill?
What advice does the speaker give students?
